# Chapter 11 — sketch answers {.unnumbered}

\(1\) First line: The web and operations team --- they run the checkout, operate
the anti-DDoS and failover controls, and own the risk of the shop going down.
Second line: The part-time security/compliance lead --- checks the protection is
configured as the policy demands, tracks R2 in the register, and challenges the
rating when facts change. Third line: The annual external reviewer ---
independently confirms the controls exist and operate, for instance by asking
for the failover test evidence. (2) Independence is what makes assurance
believable: The third line must be able to report honestly on the very
management that runs the first two lines, so it reports past them, to the
board's audit committee. Reporting to the CISO would make it a self-assessment
of the security function wearing an audit label --- structurally unable to be
candid about its own boss, and therefore worth little. (3) R: The IT lead ---
performs the restore into a test environment. A: The owner --- one name
answering that the test happened and the data came back. C: The
security/compliance lead --- consulted on scope and on what evidence to keep. I:
The web team --- informed of the result, since their recovery times depend on
it. (4) Responsible does the work and can be several people; accountable answers
for the outcome and is one person. With two accountable names, each can assume
the other is answering --- which is exactly the diffusion the scheme exists to
prevent. (5) One person holds second-line oversight and first-line operation,
and proposes to check their own work --- the three jobs collapsed into one, so
the review has no independence. Smallest fix: Keep the lead on policy and
oversight, put the monitoring's operation clearly with the first line, and buy
the once-a-year check from outside --- an external reviewer engaged by the
owner, per @tbl-fglines.
